title: Max / min whole-number answer from a word inequality
subtitle: Linear inequalities in one or two variables · 18 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **18 of the official questions in Linear inequalities in one or two variables are this one** — 6 Easy, 6 Medium, 6 Hard.
Most versions sit at the Easy tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The question asks 'what is the maximum number of …', 'the minimum number of hours', 'the greatest possible value', or 'for what values is one plan's cost greater than the other's'.
- It is often a student-produced response, and the answer is a single number or a one-sided range.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Set up the inequality: total ≤ limit, goal ≤ output, or plan A > plan B.
- If there are two item types, fill the other type's minimum requirement first so you can maximise the one asked about.
- If prices vary, use the most favourable price for the extreme case.
- 2) Solve for the variable, and flip the sign if you divide by a negative.
- 3) Round the right way for whole counts: round down for a maximum, and round up for a minimum or a strict 'more than'.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Graph each side as a function of x, e.g. y = 60x + 10 and y = 280, or the two plans' cost lines.
Click the intersection, then read which side of it satisfies the condition and apply the whole-number rounding yourself.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You round the wrong way, for example answering 5 when 4.67 hours is the cap.
You keep the boundary value when the inequality is strict.
Or you ignore a 'minimum number of items' constraint, or use the cheapest price when the extreme case needs the most expensive one.

sections.heading: You are losing these
